title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: Pierre knew this large room well—divided by columns and an arch, its walls hung with Persian carpets. The area behind the columns, with a tall silk-curtained mahogany bed on one side and an enormous icon case on the other, was bathed in red light like a Russian church during evening services. Beneath the gleaming icons stood a long reclining chair, and in it, propped on smooth white pillows that had obviously just been changed, Pierre saw the familiar, majestic figure of his father, Count Bezukhov—covered to the waist by a bright green quilt, with that gray mane of hair above his broad forehead that always made one think of a lion, and the deep, noble wrinkles of his handsome, ruddy face. He lay directly beneath the icons, his large, thick hands resting on top of the quilt. A wax taper had been placed between the forefinger and thumb of his right hand, which lay palm-down, and an old servant standing behind the chair held it in place. By the chair stood the priests, their long hair falling over magnificent, glittering vestments, holding lighted tapers and slowly, solemnly conducting the service. A little behind them stood the two younger princesses, holding handkerchiefs to their eyes. In front of them their eldest sister, Catiche, stood with a fierce and resolute expression fixed on the icons, as if declaring to everyone that she could not be held responsible for what might happen if she looked away. Anna Mikhaylovna stood by the door with a meek, sorrowful, all-forgiving expression, near the unfamiliar lady. Prince Vasili stood at the front, near the reclining chair, a wax taper in his left hand, his left arm resting on the carved back of a velvet chair he had turned around for the purpose, crossing himself with his right hand and raising his eyes heavenward each time his fingers touched his forehead. His face wore a look of calm piety and submission to God's will. "If you don't understand these feelings," his expression seemed to say, "so much the worse for you."

Behind him stood the aide-de-camp, the doctors, and the manservants. The men and women had separated as in a church. Everyone crossed themselves silently, and the only sounds were the reading of the service, the muffled chanting of deep bass voices, and in the pauses, sighs and the shuffling of feet. Anna Mikhaylovna, with an air of importance showing she knew exactly what she was doing, crossed the room to Pierre and handed him a taper. He lit it and, distracted by watching those around him, began crossing himself with the hand that held the candle.

Sophie, the rosy, youngest princess with the mole—the one who was always laughing—watched him. She smiled, buried her face in her handkerchief, and kept it hidden for a moment. Then she looked up, saw Pierre again, and couldn't help laughing once more. She clearly couldn't look at him without laughing, yet couldn't resist looking. To remove herself from temptation, she slipped quietly behind one of the columns. In the middle of the service, the priests' voices suddenly stopped. They whispered to each other, and the old servant holding the count's hand stood up and said something to the ladies. Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward and, bending over the dying man, beckoned to Lorrain from behind her back. The French doctor had no taper; he was leaning against one of the columns in a respectful posture that showed he—a foreigner—despite all differences of faith, fully understood the significance of the rite being performed and even approved of it. He now approached the sick man with the noiseless step of a person in full health, lifted the hand that lay free from the green quilt with his delicate white fingers, turned slightly to one side, and felt the pulse, reflecting for a moment. The sick man was given something to drink. There was a brief commotion around him, then everyone returned to their places and the service continued. During this pause, Pierre noticed that Prince Vasili left the chair he had been leaning on and—with an air suggesting that he knew what he was doing, and if others didn't understand, that was their problem—walked past the dying man without stopping, joined the eldest princess, and moved with her to the side of the room where the tall bed stood with its silk hangings. They both slipped out through a back door, then returned to their places one after the other before the service concluded. Pierre paid no more attention to this than to anything else going on around him, having decided once and for all that whatever was happening that evening was somehow essential.

The chanting stopped, and the priest's voice was heard respectfully congratulating the dying man on having received the sacrament. The dying man lay as lifeless and motionless as before. People began to stir around him—footsteps, whispers—among which Anna Mikhaylovna's voice was the most audible.
"He really must be moved to the bed. It's impossible here..."

The sick man was so surrounded by doctors, princesses, and servants that Pierre could no longer see the ruddy, yellowish face with its gray mane—though he hadn't lost sight of it for a single moment during the entire service, even while watching other faces. He could tell from the careful movements of those crowded around the reclining chair that they were lifting the dying man and carrying him.

"Hold onto my arm or you'll drop him!" one of the servants said in a frightened whisper. "Get a grip from underneath. Here!" voices called out, and the heavy breathing of the bearers and the scraping of their feet grew more urgent, as though the weight they carried was too much for them.

As the bearers—among them Anna Mikhaylovna—passed the young man, he caught a momentary glimpse between their heads and shoulders of the dying man's broad, uncovered chest and powerful shoulders, raised by those gripping him under the arms, and of his gray, curly, lion-like head. That head, with its remarkably wide brow and cheekbones, its handsome, sensual mouth, and its cold, majestic expression, was not disfigured by the approach of death. It looked just as Pierre remembered it from three months earlier, when the count had sent him to Petersburg. But now the head swayed helplessly with the uneven movements of the bearers, and those cold, indifferent eyes were fixed on nothing.

After a few minutes of commotion around the tall bed, the bearers dispersed. Anna Mikhaylovna touched Pierre's hand and said, "Come." Pierre went with her to the bed where the sick man had been laid in a stately pose befitting the ceremony just completed. He lay with his head propped high on the pillows, his hands placed symmetrically on the green silk quilt, palms down. When Pierre approached, the count was gazing straight at him—but with an expression whose meaning no living person could decipher. Either the look meant nothing at all, just that eyes must look somewhere as long as they exist, or it meant far too much. Pierre hesitated, unsure what to do, and glanced at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna made a quick gesture with her eyes toward the sick man's hand, moving her lips as if sending it a kiss. Pierre carefully craned his neck, trying not to touch the quilt, and pressed his lips to the large, fleshy hand with its heavy bones. Neither the hand nor a single muscle of the count's face moved. Pierre looked again at Anna Mikhaylovna, asking what to do next. She indicated a chair beside the bed with her eyes. Pierre sat down obediently, his expression silently asking whether he was doing the right thing. Anna Mikhaylovna nodded her approval. Once again Pierre assumed the naively symmetrical pose of an Egyptian statue, clearly distressed that his large, clumsy body took up so much space, doing his best to appear as small as possible. He looked at the count, who still stared at the spot where Pierre's face had been before he sat down. Anna Mikhaylovna's manner conveyed her awareness of the solemn importance of these final moments between father and son. This lasted about two minutes, though to Pierre it felt like an hour. Suddenly the broad muscles of the count's face began to twitch. The twitching grew stronger, the handsome mouth was pulled to one side—and only now did Pierre grasp how close his father was to death—and from that distorted mouth came a faint, hoarse sound. Anna Mikhaylovna watched the sick man's eyes intently, trying to read what he wanted. She pointed first to Pierre, then to a drink, then whispered Prince Vasili's name inquiringly, then pointed to the quilt. The dying man's eyes and face showed impatience. He made an effort to look at the servant who stood at the head of the bed.
"He wants to be turned onto his other side," the servant whispered, and rose to turn the count's heavy body toward the wall.

As the count was being turned, one of his arms fell back limply, and he made a futile effort to pull it forward. Whether he noticed the look of horror with which Pierre stared at that lifeless arm, or whether some other thought crossed his dying mind, he glanced at the disobedient arm, then at Pierre's terrified face, then back at the arm, and a faint, pitiful smile appeared on his face—completely at odds with his features—as though mocking his own helplessness. At the sight of that smile, Pierre felt an unexpected tremor in his chest and a prickling in his nose, and tears blurred his eyes. The sick man was turned onto his side, facing the wall. He sighed.
"He's dozing," said Anna Mikhaylovna, noticing one of the princesses coming to take her turn at the bedside watch. "Let's go."
